newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FORECAST-CZECH JULY INFLATION SEEN QUICKENING.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-CZECH JULY INFLATION SEEN QUICKENING.

text.p: Czech consumer inflation should accelerate in July, buoyed by liberalisations of rents and energy prices, a Reuter survey of analysts showed on Monday.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release July CPI data on Friday at 0700 GMT, and most economists on average forecast an increase of about 2.4 percent month-on- month, double the 1.2 percent CPI figure for June.
They said that a 50 percent rise in rents for state housing, and energy price rises of about 15 percent -- both of which took effect July 1 -- should provide most of the impetus for the increase.
"The rent increase is the highest ever, so it follows that there will be an acceleration in inflation," Boris Gomez, a macro-economic analyst at of ING Barings, told Reuters.
Many Czechs still live in flats with artificially low rents and with energy bills subsidised by industrial users.
Added Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance: "The deregulations alone will likely add about 2.5 percent points to the month-on-month rate."
Overall, prices jumped 1.2 percent month-on-month in June, forcing the year-on-year inflation rate to 6.8 percent, up from June's record low of 6.3 percent.
The sliding average inflation figure, which uses 1993 as a base, edged down to 7.9 percent from 8.0 percent in May, and was down from 8.6 percent in June 1996.
Analysts said the July year-on-year inflation rate should edge up to around 9.0 percent.
Another factor which could push the July figure higher is the lingering effects from a crisis in the Czech crown, analysts said.
The crown came under heavy downward pressure at the end of May as speculators targeted the currency as overvalued, and the ruling coalition government teetered near a possible collapse.
The CNB was eventually forced on May 27 to float the currency and abandon its 15 percent fluctuation band within which it would fix the currency against a mark/dollar peg.
The crown has since lost nearly 15 percent against the dollar, driving import prices higher.

"It's difficult to estimate the precise effect the deregulation will have. The effect of the weaker crown will be less than in June, with much of it already built into (consumer) prices," said Martin Hlucek of Expandia Finance.
